notes.title: Choosing the route for this patient

lines.text: A drug must be given, and the patient's state decides how: conscious or not, vomiting, in shock, needing an effect in seconds or over days.
Conscious, can swallow, not urgent → oral: safest, cheapest, easiest.
Emergency, unconscious, vomiting, or drug destroyed in the gut → parenteral (IV fastest).
Child vomiting with fever, or unconscious patient → rectal suppository (e.g. paracetamol).
Needs to skip the liver and act in minutes (angina) → sublingual.
Lungs are the target (asthma) → inhalation.
Slow, steady effect for hours or days → transdermal patch (nicotine, nitroglycerin, scopolamine).
Local vaginal problem → pessary (e.g. miconazole).

sections.title: What you notice → what it means

lines.text: Patient in shock → skin blood flow falls, so SC injections are barely absorbed.
Irritant drug → not SC (skin is full of nerves); give IM or IV.
Insulin or penicillin G by mouth → destroyed in the gut.
IM: deep into muscle (deltoid, gluteus). SC: only non-irritant drugs.
IV: drug acts at once, so there is little time to reverse a mistake; check the dose carefully.
Sublingual: tablet under the tongue until dissolved; don't swallow it.
Oral drugs pass through the liver first (first-pass), so part is destroyed before reaching the blood.
Sublingual and rectal blood goes straight into the circulation, avoiding most first-pass.
Oral route in an unconscious or vomiting patient: never correct.
IV bioavailability is always 100%; every other route is less.
A 3-year-old child has a high fever and keeps vomiting. Which route is most appropriate for paracetamol?
a. Oral syrup ✗: she will vomit it.
b. Rectal suppository ✓: works when vomiting; suitable for children.
c. Subcutaneous injection ✗: paracetamol isn't given SC.
d. Transdermal patch ✗: too slow; no paracetamol patch.

notes.title: Food, milk & other drugs: why absorption changes

lines.text: A drug isn't working as expected, or the nurse must decide whether to give it with food. What is in the stomach changes how much drug gets in.
Empty stomach → faster absorption.
Irritant drugs (aspirin, iron) → give after food.
Tetracycline → not with milk or antacids (calcium blocks it).
Iron → give with vitamin C, which increases absorption.
Laxatives speed the gut, so other drugs (especially slow-release) are absorbed less.
Weak acids (aspirin) absorb in the stomach; weak bases (pethidine) in the small intestine.

sections.title: What you notice → what it means

lines.text: Heart failure or liver cirrhosis → absorption and bioavailability change.
Elderly → slower stomach emptying, less blood flow; children → different stomach pH and leaky barriers.
Only the un-ionized (fat-soluble) form crosses gut membranes easily.
The intestine absorbs more than the stomach because it has far more blood flow.
Bioavailability = the part of the dose that reaches the blood; 70 mg of a 100 mg oral dose = 70%.
Nitroglycerin swallowed: over 90% destroyed by first pass, so it's given sublingually.
Food sometimes HELPS absorption (griseofulvin, propranolol).
A patient takes tetracycline with a glass of milk every morning, and the infection isn't improving. What is the most likely reason?
a. The dose is too high ✗: a high dose wouldn't cause failure.
b. Calcium in milk binds tetracycline and reduces absorption ✓: milk and antacids form insoluble complexes with tetracycline.
c. Milk speeds up the stomach ✗: that's not the mechanism.
d. Tetracycline only works by injection ✗: it's an oral drug.

notes.title: Special patients: newborns, elderly, liver & kidney disease

lines.text: The same dose can be safe in one patient and toxic in another. Age, liver and kidney function, and protein levels change how drugs are handled.
Newborn → immature liver: chloramphenicol causes gray baby syndrome.
Elderly → slower liver metabolism and kidney excretion: start low, watch for toxicity.
Liver disease or heart failure → less liver blood flow, slower metabolism → drugs build up.
Kidney disease → drugs excreted by the kidney build up; reduce doses (e.g. ethambutol, gentamicin).
Slow acetylators → more side effects from INH, hydralazine, dapsone, procainamide.

sections.title: What you notice → what it means

lines.text: Low albumin → more FREE drug for drugs carried by albumin → stronger effect.
Meningitis → the blood-brain barrier leaks, so drugs that normally can't enter the brain now can.
Some drugs collect in tissues: gentamicin in kidney, chloroquine in liver, tetracycline in bone and teeth, thiopental in fat.
Only unbound drug works and can be excreted.
The liver turns fat-soluble drugs into water-soluble forms the kidney can excrete.
Half-life gets LONGER when liver or kidney blood flow falls.
Alkalinizing urine speeds excretion of weak acids (aspirin, barbiturates); acidifying urine helps weak bases.
A newborn treated with chloramphenicol becomes pale, cyanosed and floppy. What is the most likely cause?
a. Normal newborn jaundice ✗: this picture is a drug toxicity.
b. Gray baby syndrome from immature liver metabolism ✓: newborns can't metabolize chloramphenicol.
c. Allergy to chloramphenicol ✗: allergy causes rash or anaphylaxis, not this.
d. Underdosing ✗: it's a toxicity from accumulation.

notes.title: Drug interactions: inducers, inhibitors & synergy

lines.text: A patient starts a new drug and an old one suddenly fails or becomes toxic. Usually one drug changed how the liver handles the other.
Enzyme INDUCERS (rifampin, phenobarbital, phenytoin, carbamazepine) → other drugs cleared faster → they fail.
Rifampin or phenobarbital + oral contraceptive → pill failure → unwanted pregnancy.
Enzyme INHIBITORS (cimetidine, erythromycin, isoniazid) → other drugs build up → toxicity.
Cimetidine + warfarin → warfarin rises → bleeding.
Alcohol + sedatives (benzodiazepines, barbiturates, antihistamines) → synergy → dangerous CNS depression.
Antacids or milk + tetracycline → less absorbed.
Additive: 1 + 1 = 2. Synergistic: 1 + 1 = 3. Antagonistic: 1 + 1 < 2.
Inducers make the liver produce more CYP450 enzymes; inhibitors compete for them.
Ethanol and phenytoin follow zero-order kinetics: a fixed AMOUNT is removed per hour, so they can suddenly build up to toxic levels.
Erythromycin, isoniazid or fluoxetine with carbamazepine → carbamazepine toxicity after a few days.
A woman on combined oral contraceptives is started on rifampin for TB. What is the most important teaching?
a. Take the pill with food ✗: doesn't solve the problem.
b. Use an additional or different contraceptive method ✓: rifampin induces liver enzymes and makes the pill fail.
c. Stop TB treatment while on the pill ✗: TB treatment must continue.
d. No change is needed ✗: the pill may fail.

notes.title: Half-life, steady state & loading dose

lines.text: A drug must reach a target level and stay there. Half-life decides how often to give it; a loading dose gets there faster.
Needs a level quickly → loading dose (large first dose), then maintenance doses.
Maintenance dose = what the body removes each day.
Narrow therapeutic index (digoxin, warfarin, phenytoin, lithium) → monitor blood levels.
Big swings between peaks and troughs → continuous infusion, or smaller doses more often.
Half-life: time for the blood level to fall by half. It decides the dosing interval and time to steady state.
Steady state: repeated doses reach a plateau where elimination equals the dose given.
First-order (most drugs): a fixed FRACTION is removed per hour. Zero-order (ethanol, phenytoin): a fixed AMOUNT.
Therapeutic index = toxic dose ÷ effective dose. HIGHER means SAFER.
Warfarin has a narrow index (risky); penicillin a wide one (safe).
Which drug most needs regular blood-level monitoring?
a. Paracetamol at normal doses ✗: wide safety margin at normal doses.
b. Digoxin ✓: narrow therapeutic index; toxic dose close to effective dose.
c. Penicillin ✗: wide therapeutic index.
d. Vitamin C ✗: very safe.

notes.title: Agonists, antagonists & antidotes

lines.text: Many emergencies are solved by a drug that blocks or opposes another. Knowing the type of antagonism tells you which antidote works.
Competitive antagonist (same receptor): naloxone for opioids, flumazenil for benzodiazepines, atropine for acetylcholine.
Chemical antagonist (binds the poison itself): dimercaprol for mercury, arsenic, gold.
Functional (physiological) antagonist (opposite effect on another receptor): adrenaline reverses histamine bronchospasm in anaphylaxis.
Partial agonist (pentazocine) given to someone on a full agonist (morphine) → can block it and cause withdrawal.
Potency = how little drug you need. Efficacy = the biggest effect possible. Efficacy matters more.
Agonist: affinity + activity. Antagonist: affinity, no activity.
A more potent drug isn't necessarily better; a more efficacious one is.
Antacids don't use receptors; they neutralize acid chemically.
A child swallowed a mercury-containing substance. Which antidote acts by chemical antagonism?
a. Atropine ✗: competitive antagonist at muscarinic receptors.
b. Dimercaprol ✓: binds the metal directly and removes it.
c. Naloxone ✗: competitive antagonist at opioid receptors.
d. Adrenaline ✗: functional antagonist of histamine.

notes.title: Is this an adverse drug reaction? Which type?

lines.text: A patient develops a new problem after a drug. Decide whether it's expected, dose-related, allergic or genetic, then act and report.
Expected effect at a normal dose (sedation from antihistamines) → side effect.
Too much of the drug's own effect (bleeding with warfarin, hypoglycemia with insulin) → type A, dose-related; 75% of ADRs.
Immune reaction, not dose-related (rash, anaphylaxis) → allergy, type B.
Genetic, unusual reaction (aplastic anemia with chloramphenicol) → idiosyncrasy, type B.
Toxic effects at a NORMAL dose in one sensitive person → intolerance.
Long-term use (NSAID kidney damage) → type C. Delayed (thalidomide birth defects) → type D. On stopping (β-blocker rebound) → type E.
Type B reactions: stop the drug immediately.
Report every suspected ADR (pharmacovigilance).
Record the allergy clearly so the drug is never given again.
Grade it: minor, moderate, severe (life-threatening or permanent damage), lethal.

sections.title: What you notice → what it means

lines.text: Higher risk: many drugs at once, elderly, children, pregnancy, malnutrition, multiple diseases.
Steroids weaken immunity and latent TB activates → secondary effect.
A side effect can be useful elsewhere: codeine's constipation helps diarrhea.
Stopping steroids suddenly → acute adrenal insufficiency (withdrawal reaction).
A patient on chloramphenicol develops aplastic anemia, though the dose was normal and few people react this way. This is best described as:
a. Side effect ✗: side effects are common and expected.
b. Idiosyncrasy ✓: a genetically determined abnormal reaction.
c. Overdose ✗: the dose was normal.
d. Tolerance ✗: tolerance means a reduced response.

notes.title: Drug allergy & anaphylaxis

lines.text: Minutes after a drug (often an injection), the patient has itching, rash, swelling, wheeze or low BP. This is an allergic reaction, and it can kill.
Anaphylaxis (type I) → adrenaline is the first drug.
Allergy can happen with a tiny dose, unrelated to how the drug normally works.
Aspirin allergy → avoid ALL NSAIDs.
Stop the drug; call for help; airway, breathing, circulation.
Give IM adrenaline as ordered; lay the patient flat with legs raised (unless breathless).
Before giving any drug, ask about allergies and record them.
Observe after giving drugs known to cause allergy (e.g. penicillin injections).
The drug acts as an antigen (or hapten) and triggers antibodies or sensitized cells.
Type I anaphylactic, II cytolytic, III immune complex (Arthus), IV delayed cell-mediated.
Photosensitivity: phototoxic = sunburn-like (UVB); photoallergic = eczema-like rash (UVA) with sulfonamides, chloroquine, chlorpromazine.
Adrenaline reverses bronchospasm by functional antagonism, not by blocking histamine.
Five minutes after an IM penicillin injection, a patient has wheeze, swollen lips and BP 80/50. What is the priority drug?
a. Oral antihistamine ✗: too slow and too weak for anaphylaxis.
b. Adrenaline ✓: first-line treatment of anaphylactic shock.
c. Paracetamol ✗: no role.
d. Salbutamol inhaler alone ✗: doesn't treat the shock.

notes.title: Tolerance, dependence & withdrawal

lines.text: A patient needs more drug for the same effect, or gets sick when it stops. Decide whether it's tolerance, dependence, or a withdrawal reaction.
Same dose works less over time → tolerance.
Body needs the drug to function; stopping causes withdrawal → physical dependence (opioids, alcohol, barbiturates, benzodiazepines).
Only mild discomfort on stopping (tea, coffee, tobacco) → habituation (psychological dependence).
Compulsive use that takes over life → addiction.
Taper long-term drugs: steroids, β-blockers, clonidine, benzodiazepines, antiepileptics.
lines.ref: Gen slide 127, CVS p.43, CVS p.143

lines.text: Opioid overdose → naloxone; benzodiazepine overdose → flumazenil.
Stopping steroids suddenly → adrenal crisis.
Stopping antiepileptics suddenly → status epilepticus.
Opioid tolerance develops to pain relief and breathing depression, but NOT to pinpoint pupils or constipation.
A patient on prednisolone for 6 months stops it suddenly. Two days later he is weak, dizzy and hypotensive. What is happening?
a. Steroid overdose ✗: he stopped the drug.
b. Acute adrenal insufficiency from sudden withdrawal ✓: steroids must be tapered.
c. Allergic reaction ✗: no allergic features.
d. Tolerance ✗: tolerance is a reduced response while taking the drug.

notes.title: Drugs in pregnancy: when and which harm the baby

lines.text: A pregnant woman (or a woman who might be pregnant) needs a drug. The stage of pregnancy and the drug decide the risk to the baby.
Days 18–55 (organ formation) → the most dangerous time for malformations.
Days 0–17 → the pregnancy may fail, often unnoticed.
Avoid: ACE inhibitors, ARBs, warfarin, thalidomide, valproate, phenytoin, carbamazepine, retinoids, misoprostol, statins.
lines.ref: Gen slide 128, CVS p.86, CNS slide 117, Derm p.11, GI slide 12, CVS p.159

lines.text: Safer choices: methyldopa for BP, paracetamol for pain and fever (short-term).
Aspirin and NSAIDs → avoid in the third trimester.
Before giving any drug to a woman of childbearing age, ask about pregnancy.
Use one drug at the lowest effective dose when a drug is necessary (e.g. epilepsy).
Phenytoin → cleft lip and palate.
Thalidomide → phocomelia (flipper-like limbs).
Benzodiazepines before delivery can depress the newborn's breathing.
At 6 weeks of pregnancy, a woman asks which time is most dangerous for drug-induced birth defects. The nurse's best answer:
a. The last month ✗: growth problems, not major malformations.
b. About days 18 to 55, when organs form ✓: organogenesis is the most vulnerable period.
c. Only the first 2 weeks ✗: this period usually causes pregnancy loss rather than malformation.
d. All stages carry equal risk ✗: the risk is highest during organ formation.

notes.title: Drug names, sources & clinical trial phases

lines.text: Nurses read prescriptions, labels and drug information. Know which name to use and what each trial phase means.
Prescribe and record by the generic name (paracetamol), not the brand (Panadol).
Prescription-only: antibiotics, narcotics, psychotropics. Over the counter: vitamins, antacids, simple painkillers.
Phase I: first in humans, 20–80 healthy volunteers, finds safe dose.
Phase II: first in patients, 80–100, efficacy and best dose.
Phase III: hundreds to thousands of patients; confirms efficacy.
Phase IV: after marketing; post-marketing surveillance.

sections.title: What you notice → what it means

lines.text: Sources: plants (morphine, digoxin, atropine), animals (insulin, heparin), minerals (magnesium sulfate), microbes (penicillin), genetic engineering (human insulin).
Anticancer drugs are not tested on healthy volunteers in phase I.
Pharmacovigilance and post-marketing surveillance = phase IV.
A drug has been on the market for 2 years. A study now collects reports of rare side effects from thousands of patients. Which phase is this?
a. Phase I ✗: first-in-human, small numbers.
b. Phase II ✗: first in patients, dose-finding.
c. Phase III ✗: before approval.
d. Phase IV ✓: post-marketing surveillance.

notes.title: Predicting a drug's effects from the receptor

lines.text: If you know what each receptor does, you can predict almost every ANS drug's effect and side effects without memorizing lists.
Blocks muscarinic (M3) receptors → dry mouth, dilated pupils, blurred near vision, urine retention, constipation, fast heart → “atropine pattern”.
Too much acetylcholine → salivation, tears, sweating, urination, diarrhea, pinpoint pupils, slow heart, wheeze → “cholinergic pattern”.
Stimulates β1 → faster, stronger heart; more renin.
Stimulates β2 → bronchodilation, relaxed uterus and bladder, muscle vessels dilate.
Blocks β2 (non-selective β-blocker) → bronchospasm: dangerous in asthma.
Stimulates α1 → vessels constrict, BP rises, pupil dilates, bladder sphincter closes.
Blocks α1 → BP falls on standing, urine flows more easily.
Sympathetic (“fight or flight”) uses noradrenaline on α and β receptors. Parasympathetic (“rest and digest”) uses acetylcholine on muscarinic receptors.
Pinpoint pupils + sweating + salivation → cholinergic, not opioid.
Elderly man on an anticholinergic who suddenly can't urinate → urine retention from M3 block.
A patient took an overdose of an antimuscarinic drug. Which set of findings is expected?
a. Pinpoint pupils, salivation, slow pulse ✗: that's the cholinergic pattern.
b. Dilated pupils, dry mouth, fast pulse, urine retention ✓: the atropine (antimuscarinic) pattern.
c. Wheeze, diarrhea, sweating ✗: cholinergic signs.
d. Low BP with slow pulse ✗: not typical of antimuscarinics.

notes.title: The organophosphate-poisoned patient

lines.text: A farmer, or someone who drank insecticide, arrives with too much acetylcholine everywhere: wet, slow and small.

sections.title: What you notice → what it means

lines.text: Insecticide exposure (malathion, parathion, diazinon) → organophosphate.
Salivation, tearing, sweating, urination, diarrhea, vomiting, wheeze, airway secretions → muscarinic overload.
Pinpoint pupils + slow pulse + wet patient → acetylcholine excess, not an opioid.
Muscle twitching then weakness → nicotinic effect on muscles.
Airway first: suction secretions, oxygen, support breathing.
Decontaminate: remove clothes, wash the skin.
Atropine: the cornerstone; repeat until secretions dry.
Pralidoxime (2-PAM) early, before the enzyme “ages”.
Organophosphates bind acetylcholinesterase permanently, so acetylcholine floods every synapse.
Atropine blocks the muscarinic effects; pralidoxime frees the enzyme, but only before aging.
Neostigmine or physostigmine: also cholinesterase inhibitors → worse.
Naloxone for the pinpoint pupils: wrong; opioids don't cause salivation, sweating and diarrhea.
Adrenaline: for anaphylaxis and cardiac arrest, not this.
A 40-year-old farmer arrives 1 hour after spraying insecticide: drooling, sweating, wheezing, pinpoint pupils, pulse 48. Which drug is the priority?
a. Atropine ✓: blocks the excess acetylcholine; the cornerstone.
b. Neostigmine ✗: another cholinesterase inhibitor; makes it worse.
c. Adrenaline ✗: not for cholinergic poisoning.
d. Naloxone ✗: reverses opioids; this picture is cholinergic.

notes.title: Myasthenia, urine retention & glaucoma: cholinergic drugs

lines.text: Drugs that boost acetylcholine help when muscles, bladder or eye drainage need more parasympathetic push.
Myasthenia gravis, long-term → pyridostigmine (or neostigmine).
Diagnosing myasthenia → edrophonium (very short-acting).
Reversing non-depolarizing muscle relaxants after surgery → neostigmine.
Atropine (anticholinergic) overdose → physostigmine; it reaches the brain.
Urine retention after surgery or delivery, no obstruction → bethanechol.
Acute angle-closure glaucoma → pilocarpine (plus other drugs); iridectomy is the definitive treatment.
Open-angle glaucoma first line → prostaglandin analogue, timolol, or a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor.
Alzheimer's → donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine (slow it, can't stop it).
Pilocarpine contracts the ciliary muscle and iris sphincter, opening the drainage meshwork, so eye pressure falls.
Bethanechol with a blocked urethra (obstruction): wrong; it's for non-obstructive retention only.
Too much cholinesterase inhibitor → muscle weakness and paralysis too.
A woman cannot pass urine 8 hours after a normal delivery. The bladder is distended and there is no obstruction. Which drug might be ordered?
a. Atropine ✗: would worsen retention.
b. Bethanechol ✓: stimulates the bladder in non-obstructive retention.
c. Prazosin ✗: used in men with prostate enlargement.
d. Oxybutynin ✗: treats overactive bladder; worsens retention.

notes.title: Atropine & other anticholinergics: uses and toxicity

lines.text: Atropine-like drugs dry secretions, speed the heart and relax smooth muscle. Each relative has a special use, and all share the same toxicity.
Bradycardia, or before surgery to dry secretions → atropine.
Organophosphate poisoning → atropine.
Eye exam (dilate pupil) → tropicamide (6 h) or cyclopentolate (24 h).
Motion sickness, post-operative nausea → scopolamine.
COPD maintenance, acute asthma add-on → inhaled ipratropium or tiotropium.
Tremor and stiffness from antipsychotics, Parkinsonism → benztropine or trihexyphenidyl.
Overactive bladder → oxybutynin, tolterodine.

sections.title: What you notice → what it means

lines.text: Dry mouth, blurred vision, fast pulse, urine retention, constipation → anticholinergic side effects.
Confusion, hallucinations, delirium → anticholinergic toxicity (especially elderly).
Atropine overdose → physostigmine.
Watch the elderly for urine retention and confusion.
Avoid in narrow-angle glaucoma and prostate enlargement.
Scopolamine causes sedation and memory loss; it can be abused.
Ipratropium works on the lungs without the full atropine effects (quaternary drug).
An elderly man becomes confused and can't pass urine after starting an anticholinergic. His pupils are dilated and his mouth is dry. What is the best explanation?
a. Stroke ✗: the drug explains every finding.
b. Anticholinergic toxicity ✓: classic dry, retention, dilated pupils, confusion.
c. Cholinergic crisis ✗: would cause small pupils and secretions.
d. Dehydration only ✗: doesn't explain the pupils and retention.

notes.title: Muscle relaxants in surgery

lines.text: During anesthesia, muscle relaxants paralyze skeletal muscle for intubation and surgery. The nurse knows how each ends and what can go wrong.
Rapid intubation (risk of aspiration) or ECT → succinylcholine, fastest onset.
Longer surgery → non-depolarizing (rocuronium, vecuronium, atracurium).
Reverse non-depolarizing relaxants → neostigmine.

sections.title: What you notice → what it means

lines.text: High fever, rigidity during anesthesia with halothane + succinylcholine → malignant hyperthermia.
Patient doesn't breathe for hours after succinylcholine → pseudocholinesterase deficiency.
High potassium after succinylcholine.
Malignant hyperthermia → dantrolene.
Keep ventilation support ready until the relaxant wears off.
Aminoglycosides, CCBs and inhaled anesthetics make the block stronger; report if the patient is on them.
Neostigmine reverses NON-depolarizing relaxants, not succinylcholine.
These drugs paralyze but don't sedate or relieve pain.
During surgery under halothane and succinylcholine, the patient's temperature rises to 41 °C with muscle rigidity. Which drug is needed?
a. Paracetamol ✗: doesn't treat malignant hyperthermia.
b. Dantrolene ✓: the specific treatment.
c. Neostigmine ✗: reverses non-depolarizing relaxants.
d. More succinylcholine ✗: worsens it.

notes.title: Shock, anaphylaxis & cardiac arrest: adrenergic drugs

lines.text: A patient is in shock, anaphylaxis or cardiac arrest. Sympathomimetic drugs raise BP, support the heart and open the airways.
Anaphylactic shock → adrenaline.
Cardiac arrest or complete heart block → adrenaline.
Shock with poor kidney blood flow → low-dose dopamine (2–5 μg/kg/min).
Acute heart failure needing a stronger heartbeat → dobutamine.
Hypotension during surgery, especially with a fast heart rate → phenylephrine.
Noradrenaline leaked into tissue → phentolamine to prevent necrosis.

sections.title: What you notice → what it means

lines.text: Adrenaline side effects: arrhythmia, angina, anxiety, tremor, high blood sugar.
High-dose dopamine (10–30 μg/kg/min) → vasoconstriction, less kidney blood flow.
Adrenaline: IV, IM or SC; not by mouth.
Check IV sites often during vasopressor infusions.
Diabetics on adrenaline may need more insulin.
Patient on propranolol given adrenaline → BP can rise sharply (α effect unopposed).
Adrenaline is added to local anesthetics to prolong them, but avoided in heart disease.
Dopamine: 2–5 μg/kg/min kidney; 5–10 heart (β1); 10–30 vessels (α1).
A patient's noradrenaline infusion leaks into the tissue of the forearm, which turns pale and cold. Which drug should be prepared?
a. Phentolamine ✓: reverses the vasoconstriction and prevents necrosis.
b. Adrenaline ✗: worsens vasoconstriction.
c. Dopamine ✗: also a vasopressor.
d. Atropine ✗: no role here.

notes.title: Asthma attack: β2 agonists & friends

lines.text: A patient with asthma is wheezing and breathless. Fast airway openers come first; some heart and BP drugs make asthma worse.
Acute attack → inhaled short-acting β2 agonist (salbutamol); works in 1–5 minutes.
Add inhaled ipratropium in acute asthma; tiotropium for COPD maintenance.
Severe attack with shock signs → adrenaline.
Long-acting β2 agonists (salmeterol, formoterol) → maintenance, not rescue.

sections.title: What you notice → what it means

lines.text: Tremor and fast heart rate after salbutamol → expected β effects.
Wheeze after starting propranolol → non-selective β-blocker bronchospasm.
Teach correct inhaler use: shake, breathe out, inhale slowly while pressing, hold the breath.
Sit the patient upright; give oxygen as ordered.
Asthma + propranolol → contraindicated.
Ephedrine also opens airways but is now rarely used.
A 20-year-old with known asthma has an acute attack with wheeze and breathlessness. Which drug gives the fastest relief?
a. Inhaled salbutamol ✓: short-acting β2 agonist; acts in minutes.
b. Oral prednisolone ✗: takes hours.
c. Inhaled salmeterol ✗: long-acting; for maintenance.
d. Propranolol ✗: causes bronchospasm.

notes.title: β-blockers: who should get them, who shouldn't

lines.text: β-blockers slow and calm the heart. The decision is whether this patient is a good candidate or at risk.
Indications: angina, arrhythmias, hypertension, chronic heart failure (carvedilol, metoprolol, bisoprolol), migraine, anxiety, hyperthyroidism, portal hypertension, glaucoma (timolol).
Asthma or COPD → avoid non-selective (propranolol); a cardioselective one (atenolol, metoprolol) only with caution.
Bradycardia, hypotension, AV block, acute decompensated heart failure → contraindicated.
Diabetic on insulin → β-blockers hide the warning signs of hypoglycemia.
Check pulse and BP before each dose; hold and report if the pulse is very slow.
Never stop suddenly: rebound tachycardia, hypertension, even MI.
Teach diabetics to check blood sugar more often.

sections.title: What you notice → what it means

lines.text: Cold hands, fatigue, nightmares, impotence → common β-blocker side effects.
Esmolol has the shortest half-life (10 min); used IV.
Carvedilol and labetalol block both α1 and β.
Not useful in variant (spasm) angina.
Which patient should NOT receive propranolol?
a. A man with stage fright before speaking ✗: a common use.
b. A woman with asthma ✓: non-selective β-blockers cause bronchospasm.
c. A patient with migraine ✗: propranolol prevents migraine.
d. A patient with hyperthyroid tremor ✗: reduces symptoms.

notes.title: α-blockers & α-agonists

lines.text: α1-blockers relax vessels and the prostate; α-agonists squeeze vessels. Choose by the target organ.
Enlarged prostate (BPH) → tamsulosin (fewer BP effects) or prazosin.
Hypertension with BPH → prazosin.
Pheochromocytoma BP crisis, or noradrenaline leak → phentolamine.
Blocked nose, eye redness → oxymetazoline or phenylephrine (short-term).
Hypertension in pregnancy → methyldopa (α2-agonist).

sections.title: What you notice → what it means

lines.text: Dizziness or fainting on standing after the first prazosin dose → first-dose orthostatic hypotension.
Nose blocked again after weeks of decongestant spray → rebound congestion.
Give the first α-blocker dose at bedtime; rise slowly.
Limit decongestant sprays to a few days.
Phenylephrine raises BP, which causes a reflex SLOW heart rate.
Yohimbine (α2-blocker) does the opposite of clonidine: raises BP and heart rate.
A 68-year-old man starts prazosin for prostate enlargement. What is the most important teaching about the first dose?
a. Take it in the morning with breakfast ✗: fainting risk while active.
b. Take it at bedtime and get up slowly ✓: first-dose orthostatic hypotension.
c. Double the dose if urine doesn't improve ✗: unsafe.
d. Avoid fluids ✗: not relevant.

notes.title: Anxiety & insomnia: choosing the drug

lines.text: A patient can't sleep, or is very anxious. The right drug depends on how fast relief is needed, how long it's needed, and the risk of dependence.
Severe anxiety, short-term, quick relief → benzodiazepine (diazepam, lorazepam, alprazolam).
Long-term generalized anxiety, no sedation or addiction wanted → buspirone (takes weeks) or an SSRI.
Simple insomnia → zolpidem or zaleplon (disturb sleep stages less) or a short course of a benzodiazepine.
Trouble falling asleep, no abuse risk wanted → ramelteon.
Stage fright with tremor and palpitations → β-blocker (propranolol).
Before endoscopy or a procedure (sedation + amnesia) → midazolam.
Hypnotics: limit to 2–4 weeks.

sections.title: What you notice → what it means

lines.text: Daytime drowsiness, hangover, unsteadiness, amnesia → benzodiazepine side effects.
Elderly patient falls at night after a sleeping pill → sedative-induced unsteadiness.
Warn: no alcohol, no driving until she knows how the drug affects her.
Use the lowest dose for the shortest time; taper when stopping.
Use cautiously in the elderly and in liver or kidney disease.
Benzodiazepines make GABA work better (more chloride into neurons → calmer brain). Low dose calms, higher dose brings sleep.
Buspirone for a panic attack: wrong; it takes weeks to work.
Benzodiazepines in pregnancy or near delivery → may depress the newborn.
Benzodiazepine + alcohol → possibly fatal CNS depression.
A 35-year-old woman has had generalized anxiety for a year. She drives a taxi and fears becoming addicted to pills. Which drug is most appropriate for long-term treatment?
a. Diazepam ✗: sedating and causes dependence long-term.
b. Buspirone ✓: non-sedating, no dependence; suits long-term anxiety.
c. Phenobarbital ✗: sedating and addictive.
d. Midazolam ✗: for procedures, not long-term anxiety.

notes.title: Sedative overdose & withdrawal

lines.text: A patient is drowsy or unconscious after too many sleeping pills, or shaking and seizing after stopping them. Know the antidote and the danger.
Benzodiazepine overdose → support breathing; flumazenil IV reverses it.
Barbiturate overdose → NO antidote: support breathing, empty the stomach if recent, alkalinize urine, hemodialysis if severe.
Sudden stop after long benzodiazepine use → withdrawal like alcohol (seizures, fever, delirium) → taper slowly.

sections.title: What you notice → what it means

lines.text: Short-acting benzodiazepines (triazolam) → worse withdrawal than long-acting ones.
Seizures after flumazenil → flumazenil can trigger seizures.
Airway first: position, suction, oxygen; monitor breathing rate.
Flumazenil is short-acting (~1 hour): watch for re-sedation; repeat doses may be needed.
Flumazenil for a barbiturate overdose: doesn't work.
Barbiturates cause tolerance faster than benzodiazepines, and their withdrawal can kill.
A patient is brought in drowsy with slow breathing after swallowing many diazepam tablets. After securing the airway, which drug reverses the effect?
a. Naloxone ✗: reverses opioids.
b. Flumazenil ✓: benzodiazepine antagonist.
c. Atropine ✗: no role.
d. Physostigmine ✗: for anticholinergic overdose.

notes.title: Alcohol: withdrawal, disulfiram & methanol

lines.text: An alcoholic patient is admitted: withdrawal may start, they may want help to stop drinking, or someone drank home-made alcohol.
Alcohol withdrawal → benzodiazepine (chlordiazepoxide, diazepam) is the treatment of choice.
Withdrawal seizures → carbamazepine can help.
Wants to stop drinking, will take daily tablet → disulfiram (drinking becomes unpleasant).
Craving, better tolerated option → naltrexone with counselling.
Methanol poisoning (blurred vision, acidosis) → fomepizole.

sections.title: What you notice → what it means

lines.text: Flushing, fast heart, nausea, breathlessness after a drink on disulfiram → disulfiram reaction.
Same reaction with alcohol on metronidazole → disulfiram-like reaction.
Teach: no alcohol at all on disulfiram or metronidazole, including alcohol in mouthwash or syrups.
Disulfiram contraindications: heart disease, psychosis, metronidazole, recent alcohol.
Disulfiram given to someone who is still drunk: dangerous.
Alcohol multiplies the effect of benzodiazepines, antihistamines and barbiturates.
A patient treated with metronidazole drinks beer and develops flushing, palpitations and vomiting. What explains this?
a. Allergy to metronidazole ✗: this is a drug-alcohol interaction.
b. Disulfiram-like reaction ✓: acetaldehyde builds up.
c. Alcohol withdrawal ✗: he just drank.
d. Methanol poisoning ✗: no blurred vision or acidosis.

notes.title: Seizures: which antiepileptic for which patient

lines.text: A patient has epilepsy. The seizure type and who the patient is (child, pregnant woman) decide the drug.
Child with brief staring spells (absence) → ethosuximide or valproate. NOT carbamazepine.
Tonic-clonic seizures → valproate, phenytoin or carbamazepine.
Complex partial seizures → carbamazepine (most effective).
Myoclonic seizures → valproate (or clonazepam).
Febrile seizures (3 months–5 years) → phenobarbital or diazepam; phenytoin and carbamazepine don't work.
Pregnant → one drug at the lowest dose; phenobarbital is considered safest; avoid valproate.
Trigeminal neuralgia → carbamazepine (drug of choice).
Seizures + bipolar disorder → valproate or carbamazepine.
Never stop an antiepileptic suddenly: risk of status epilepticus. Taper.
Warn women about birth defects; plan pregnancy.
Follow blood levels; add a second drug only if the first fails at full dose.
Valproate in a child under 3 → risk of fatal liver failure.
Clonazepam + valproate → can trigger absence status.
A 7-year-old girl has many brief episodes a day of blank staring and eye blinking, without falling. Which drug is most appropriate?
a. Carbamazepine ✗: can worsen absence seizures.
b. Ethosuximide ✓: used only for absence seizures; first choice.
c. Phenytoin ✗: not effective for absence seizures.
d. Phenobarbital ✗: not the drug of choice for absence.

notes.title: Status epilepticus: what to do first

lines.text: A patient seizes continuously, or has seizure after seizure without waking. This is an emergency that can damage the brain and kill.
First drug → IV lorazepam or diazepam (fast).
Then a longer-acting drug → phenytoin or fosphenytoin IV.
Give these slowly to avoid respiratory depression and apnea.
Protect the patient from injury; don't restrain; nothing in the mouth.
Turn on the side; clear the airway; give oxygen.
Time the seizure; check blood glucose.
Watch breathing closely after IV benzodiazepines.

sections.title: What you notice → what it means

lines.text: Common triggers: stopping antiepileptics suddenly, alcohol or sedative withdrawal, low blood sugar, fever, head injury.
Phenytoin alone first: too slow; a benzodiazepine comes first.
IV phenytoin can cause severe hypotension and arrhythmias; give slowly with monitoring.
A man with epilepsy has been seizing for 10 minutes without regaining consciousness. After airway and oxygen, which drug comes first?
a. Oral carbamazepine ✗: can't swallow; too slow.
b. IV lorazepam or diazepam ✓: fast-acting first line in status epilepticus.
c. IV phenytoin alone ✗: given after the benzodiazepine.
d. Paracetamol ✗: no role.

notes.title: Antiepileptic side effects & interactions

lines.text: A patient on antiepileptics comes with a new problem: gums, blood count, rash, liver, or a drug that stopped working. Match it to the drug.
Overgrown gums, nystagmus, unsteadiness, coarse face → phenytoin.
Megaloblastic anemia (folate) and soft bones (vitamin D) → phenytoin.
Low WBC or aplastic anemia, low sodium in the elderly → carbamazepine; monitor blood counts.
Liver failure (children under 3), hair loss, low platelets, bleeding → valproate.
New rash → lamotrigine: think Stevens-Johnson syndrome.
Drowsiness, lower IQ in children → phenobarbital.
Kidney stones, weight loss, slowed thinking → topiramate.

sections.title: What you notice → what it means

lines.text: Phenytoin, carbamazepine, phenobarbital speed up the liver → pill failure, weaker warfarin.
Isoniazid, cimetidine, erythromycin raise phenytoin or carbamazepine → toxicity.
Valproate raises phenobarbital and frees phenytoin from proteins → toxicity.
Good mouth care and dental visits on phenytoin.
Monitor blood counts (carbamazepine), liver tests (valproate) and drug levels.
Women on enzyme inducers need another contraceptive method.
Phenytoin follows zero-order kinetics: a small dose increase can cause big toxicity.
A 25-year-old on phenytoin for 2 years has swollen, overgrown gums. What is the most likely cause?
a. Vitamin C deficiency ✗: the drug is the classic cause.
b. Phenytoin side effect (gingival hyperplasia) ✓: typical of phenytoin.
c. Valproate side effect ✗: valproate causes hair loss and liver problems.
d. Allergy ✗: allergy causes rash.

notes.title: Parkinson's & Alzheimer's drugs

lines.text: An older patient with tremor, rigidity and slow movement (Parkinson's), or memory loss (Alzheimer's). The nurse gives the drugs safely and spots interactions.
Parkinson's → levodopa + carbidopa, the most effective.
Response wears off between doses → add selegiline, entacapone, or a dopamine agonist (ropinirole, pramipexole).
Mild symptoms or tremor from antipsychotics → benztropine, trihexyphenidyl.
Alzheimer's mild–moderate → donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine.
Alzheimer's moderate–severe → memantine, often with one of the above.

sections.title: What you notice → what it means

lines.text: Nausea, vomiting, low BP, involuntary movements, hallucinations, dark urine → levodopa effects.
Insomnia on selegiline → it was given too late in the day.
Jaundice on tolcapone → liver necrosis.
Avoid pyridoxine (B6) supplements with levodopa alone; they reduce its effect.
Give selegiline in the morning or early afternoon.
Rise slowly; levodopa lowers BP.
Antipsychotics or metoclopramide in a Parkinson's patient → they block dopamine and cancel levodopa.
MAO inhibitors + levodopa → hypertensive crisis.
Alzheimer's drugs only slow decline; none stop the disease.
A Parkinson's patient on levodopa-carbidopa is vomiting. Which antiemetic should the nurse question?
a. Metoclopramide ✓: blocks dopamine and worsens Parkinson's.
b. Ondansetron ✗: doesn't block dopamine.
c. Small frequent meals ✗: a reasonable measure.
d. Taking levodopa with a snack ✗: can reduce nausea.

notes.title: Antipsychotics and their side effects

lines.text: A patient with schizophrenia or acute psychosis (hallucinations, delusions, agitation) needs an antipsychotic. Side effects are where most problems arise.
Acute schizophrenia → haloperidol (preferred typical).
Negative symptoms or resistant schizophrenia → atypical (clozapine, olanzapine).
Mania → olanzapine (alone may equal lithium/valproate + benzodiazepine).
Severe nausea and vomiting → prochlorperazine. Intractable hiccups → chlorpromazine.
Long-term treatment; most patients relapse without it.

sections.title: What you notice → what it means

lines.text: Twisted neck or face spasm (dystonia), restlessness (akathisia), tremor and stiffness → EPS from dopamine block.
Lip smacking and tongue movements after years of treatment → tardive dyskinesia.
Breast milk, enlarged breasts → high prolactin.
Fever and sore throat on clozapine → agranulocytosis: check WBC.
Weight gain, diabetes, high cholesterol → atypical antipsychotics.
Drug-induced parkinsonism → benztropine or trihexyphenidyl.
Rise slowly (low BP); avoid alcohol and other sedatives.
Explain that the effect takes days to weeks.
Typical antipsychotics help positive symptoms but little for negative ones.
Chlorpromazine and clozapine lower the seizure threshold; avoid in epilepsy.
Antipsychotics reduce the BP effect of clonidine and methyldopa.
Three days after starting haloperidol, a young man suddenly has his neck twisted to one side and his eyes rolled up. What is the most appropriate drug?
a. Benztropine ✓: treats acute dystonia (EPS).
b. More haloperidol ✗: worsens it.
c. Levodopa ✗: not used for drug-induced EPS.
d. Paracetamol ✗: no role.
A patient on clozapine has fever and a sore throat. What is the priority?
a. Give paracetamol and continue ✗: may hide agranulocytosis.
b. Hold clozapine and check the WBC count ✓: clozapine can cause agranulocytosis.
c. Start an antibiotic ✗: check WBC first.
d. Increase the dose ✗: harmful.

notes.title: Depression: choosing & monitoring antidepressants

lines.text: A patient with depression starts or changes an antidepressant. The nurse sets expectations, watches safety, and knows the dangerous combinations.
First choice → SSRI (fluoxetine, sertraline): fewer side effects, safer in overdose.
SSRI not working → SNRI (venlafaxine, duloxetine).
Neuropathic pain, migraine → amitriptyline. Bedwetting in children → imipramine.
Not responding to others → MAO inhibitor, with strict diet rules.
Switching from an MAOI → wait at least 2 weeks.

sections.title: What you notice → what it means

lines.text: No improvement after 1 week → normal; antidepressants need at least 2 weeks.
Dry mouth, constipation, urine retention, dizziness on standing, sedation → TCA side effects.
Headache and very high BP after cheese or red wine on phenelzine → tyramine hypertensive crisis.
Insomnia, anxiety, sexual problems → SSRI side effects.
Watch closely for suicidal thoughts in the first weeks, as energy returns before mood improves.
Give TCAs carefully to at-risk patients; overdose causes fatal arrhythmias.
Teach MAOI patients to avoid aged cheese, red wine and other tyramine foods.
SSRI + MAOI, or TCA + MAOI → dangerous (high fever, seizures).
Antidepressants lower the seizure threshold.
A man started fluoxetine 5 days ago and says it isn't working, so he wants to stop. What is the nurse's best response?
a. Stop it and try another drug ✗: too early to judge.
b. Antidepressants take at least 2 weeks to start working; continue ✓: effect needs time.
c. Double the dose today ✗: not the nurse's decision; not needed.
d. Add a benzodiazepine ✗: doesn't address the issue.

notes.title: Bipolar disorder & lithium

lines.text: A patient with bipolar disorder takes lithium to treat mania and prevent relapse. Lithium's safety margin is narrow, so the nurse watches for toxicity.
Acute mania and preventing bipolar relapse → lithium.
Alternatives → valproate, carbamazepine, lamotrigine, antipsychotics; benzodiazepines for acute agitation.
Thiazide, loop diuretics or NSAIDs added → lithium level rises → toxicity.

sections.title: What you notice → what it means

lines.text: Thirst, frequent urination, fine hand tremor, GI upset → common side effects.
Coarse tremor, vomiting, diarrhea, confusion, unsteadiness → lithium toxicity.
Tiredness, weight gain, feeling cold → low thyroid from lithium.
Give with food to reduce stomach upset.
Keep salt and fluid intake steady; dehydration and sweating raise the level.
Check lithium levels and thyroid function regularly.
Lithium takes about 2 weeks to work.
Hydrochlorothiazide for a patient on lithium → toxicity risk.
A woman on lithium is started on hydrochlorothiazide. A week later she has vomiting, diarrhea, a coarse tremor and confusion. What is the most likely cause?
a. Gastroenteritis ✗: the drug combination explains everything.
b. Lithium toxicity ✓: thiazides raise lithium levels.
c. Low thyroid ✗: doesn't cause these acute signs.
d. Worsening mania ✗: these are signs of toxicity.

notes.title: Pain & fever: choosing the analgesic

lines.text: A patient has pain or fever. The type of pain, age, pregnancy, stomach and allergy history decide between paracetamol, aspirin, NSAIDs and opioids.
Mild pain or fever, children, pregnancy, stomach problems, aspirin allergy → paracetamol.
Pain with inflammation (arthritis, muscle) → NSAID (ibuprofen, diclofenac) or aspirin.
Moderate to severe pain (post-op, cancer, MI, labor) → opioid (morphine).
Mild to moderate pain needing more than paracetamol → codeine, often with paracetamol.
Prevent MI and TIA → low-dose aspirin.

sections.title: What you notice → what it means

lines.text: Epigastric pain, black stools on aspirin or NSAIDs → GI ulcer and bleeding.
Ringing in the ears, dizziness, fast breathing on high-dose aspirin → salicylism.
Jaundice after paracetamol overdose or chronic use with alcohol → liver damage.
Give aspirin and NSAIDs with food.
Never exceed 4 g of paracetamol a day; less in heavy drinkers.
Aspirin and NSAIDs block COX → fewer prostaglandins → less pain, fever and inflammation; COX-1 also protects the stomach.
Paracetamol has no anti-inflammatory effect.
Child or teenager with flu or chickenpox → never aspirin (Reye's syndrome).
Aspirin allergy → avoid all NSAIDs.
Third trimester → avoid aspirin and NSAIDs.
Paracetamol: maximum 4,000 mg a day.
Aspirin: maximum 8 g a day.
A 10-year-old with chickenpox has a fever of 38.9 °C. Which drug is most appropriate?
a. Aspirin ✗: risk of Reye's syndrome in children with viral illness.
b. Paracetamol ✓: safe for fever in children.
c. Morphine ✗: not for fever.
d. Diclofenac injection ✗: not appropriate for simple fever in a child.

notes.title: Opioids: giving them safely & managing overdose

lines.text: A patient receives morphine or another opioid for severe pain. The nurse checks breathing before and after, prevents constipation, and recognizes overdose.
Overdose (coma, slow breathing, pinpoint pupils) → naloxone IV, IM or SC.
Opioid dependence → methadone; with counselling, naltrexone.
Labor epidural → fentanyl with a local anesthetic.

sections.title: What you notice → what it means

lines.text: Breathing slow and shallow → respiratory depression, the most dangerous effect.
Constipation, urine retention, nausea, low BP on standing → expected effects to manage.
Tremor, sweating, fever, dilated pupils, fast breathing after stopping → withdrawal (can start after only 3 days).
Check breathing rate and sedation before each dose; hold and report if breathing is slow.
Give a laxative with regular opioids; tolerance never develops to constipation.
Naloxone acts shorter than many opioids: keep watching for return of sedation.
Caution with head injury: opioids raise intracranial pressure.
Pinpoint pupils persist even with tolerance; tolerance develops to pain relief and breathing depression.
Fentanyl patches can cause fatal hypoventilation; never in opioid-naive patients.
Pentazocine (partial agonist) in someone on morphine → can block it and cause withdrawal.
Two hours after morphine, a post-operative patient is hard to wake, breathing 6/min, with pinpoint pupils. After supporting breathing, what does the nurse give?
a. Flumazenil ✗: reverses benzodiazepines.
b. Naloxone ✓: opioid antagonist; drug of choice for overdose.
c. Atropine ✗: no role.
d. Another dose of morphine ✗: dangerous.

notes.title: Anesthesia: what the nurse needs to know

lines.text: A patient goes for surgery. Several drugs are combined (balanced anesthesia), and each has a reason and a risk the nurse should know.
Premedication: benzodiazepine (anxiety), antiemetic, opioid (pain), atropine (secretions, slow heart), antihistamine, muscle relaxant.
Balanced anesthesia = premedication + IV drug to induce + inhaled drug to maintain.
Asthmatic or shocked (hypovolemic) patient → ketamine (doesn't depress breathing; raises BP).
Patient with heart disease or shock → etomidate.
Sedating an intubated patient → propofol.
Child without IV access → halothane or sevoflurane by inhalation.

sections.title: What you notice → what it means

lines.text: Vivid dreams and disorientation on waking → ketamine.
Pain at the injection site → propofol.
Laryngospasm → thiopental.
Diffusion hypoxia after nitrous oxide.
Local anesthetic with adrenaline: avoid in heart disease, arrhythmia, thyrotoxicosis, uncontrolled hypertension, and in patients on β-blockers or TCAs.
Never inject a local anesthetic into a vein by mistake; aspirate first.
Spinal anesthesia: watch BP; for lower abdomen and leg surgery.
Ketamine in a hypertensive or heart patient → dangerous.
Thiopental in porphyria → contraindicated.
Halothane relaxes the uterus → more bleeding after delivery.
A patient in hypovolemic shock with asthma needs emergency surgery. Which IV anesthetic is most suitable for induction?
a. Thiopental ✗: lowers BP; can cause laryngospasm.
b. Ketamine ✓: raises BP and doesn't depress breathing.
c. Propofol ✗: lowers BP and depresses breathing.
d. Halothane ✗: an inhaled agent; lowers BP.

notes.title: Acute stroke: drug decisions

lines.text: A patient arrives with sudden weakness or speech loss. Drug decisions depend on whether it's a clot (87%) or a bleed (13%).
First → support breathing and circulation, then CT scan to tell clot from bleed.
Acute ischemic stroke: don't lower BP unless above 220/120 or another emergency; if needed, labetalol or nicardipine.
Preventing another ischemic stroke → antiplatelet (aspirin, clopidogrel).
Stroke with atrial fibrillation → anticoagulant (warfarin) to prevent another.
Hemorrhagic stroke → no standard drug; control BP and intracranial pressure (nimodipine).
Check blood glucose; position to protect the airway; nothing by mouth until swallowing is checked.
Never give aspirin before a CT rules out bleeding.
Lowering BP aggressively in the first days of ischemic stroke → less blood to the brain, worse symptoms.
A 70-year-old has had right-sided weakness for 2 hours. BP 185/100. CT shows an ischemic stroke. What is correct about the BP?
a. Lower it quickly to 120/80 ✗: reduces brain blood flow.
b. Leave it untreated unless above 220/120 or another emergency ✓: the recommended approach.
c. Give sublingual nifedipine ✗: sudden drops are dangerous.
d. Give furosemide ✗: not the treatment.

notes.title: Choosing and watching a diuretic

lines.text: A patient has fluid overload (edema, pulmonary edema), high BP, or raised pressure in the brain or eye. The diuretic is chosen by how strong and how fast it must work, and the nurse watches the electrolytes.
Acute pulmonary edema or severe edema → loop diuretic (furosemide), the strongest.
Mild edema or everyday hypertension → thiazide (hydrochlorothiazide), once daily.
Hypertension with kidney failure → loop diuretic; thiazides work poorly when kidneys fail.
Too much aldosterone (cirrhosis, heart failure, hyperaldosteronism) → spironolactone.
Raised intracranial pressure after head injury → mannitol IV.
Glaucoma or mountain sickness → acetazolamide.
Elderly woman with osteoporosis and hypertension → thiazide (it keeps calcium).

sections.title: What you notice → what it means

lines.text: Weakness, cramps, irregular pulse on furosemide or thiazide → LOW potassium.
Ringing in the ears or hearing loss on furosemide (worse with gentamicin) → ototoxicity.
Painful big toe on a thiazide → gout from high uric acid.
High blood sugar in a diabetic on a thiazide or loop → expected metabolic effect.
Muscle weakness and arrhythmia on spironolactone + ACE inhibitor → HIGH potassium.
Breast enlargement in a man on spironolactone → gynecomastia.
Weigh daily at the same time; record intake and output; check BP.
Check potassium (and sodium, magnesium) regularly.
Give diuretics in the morning so the patient doesn't wake at night to urinate.
On loop or thiazide: encourage potassium-rich food (banana, orange) unless told otherwise. On spironolactone: avoid potassium supplements.
Give IV furosemide slowly; fast injection raises the risk of hearing damage.
Loop diuretics block salt uptake where 25–30% of salt is reabsorbed, so they remove the most water.
Thiazides act further down, where only about 5% is reabsorbed: moderate, but long-acting.
Spironolactone blocks aldosterone, so the kidney keeps potassium instead of losing it.
Loop diuretics → calcium goes DOWN. Thiazides → calcium goes UP.
Diuretic that causes acidosis → acetazolamide or spironolactone. Loops and thiazides cause alkalosis.
Low K⁺ from a diuretic makes digoxin toxic.
Oral furosemide: starts in about 30 minutes, lasts up to 6 hours.
Diuretics lower BP by about 10–15 mmHg.
A 60-year-old man is admitted with acute pulmonary edema: severe breathlessness and crackles in both lungs. Which drug will the nurse expect to give first?
a. Hydrochlorothiazide by mouth ✗: too weak and too slow for an emergency.
b. IV furosemide ✓: the strongest, fastest diuretic; the key drug in acute pulmonary edema.
c. Spironolactone ✗: weak on its own; used for aldosterone excess.
d. Acetazolamide ✗: weak diuretic; used for glaucoma.
A patient on furosemide for 2 weeks has muscle cramps, weakness and an irregular pulse. Which result does the nurse expect?
a. Potassium 2.9 mEq/L ✓: furosemide causes potassium loss.
b. Potassium 5.9 mEq/L ✗: high potassium is caused by spironolactone, not furosemide.
c. Calcium 11.5 mg/dL ✗: loop diuretics lower calcium.
d. Blood sugar 60 mg/dL ✗: diuretics tend to raise blood sugar.

notes.title: Is this hypertension? Lifestyle first

lines.text: A patient has a raised BP reading. Confirm it properly, then start lifestyle changes for everyone; add drugs if the target isn't reached.
Diagnose only after raised readings on two different days.
Lifestyle changes are for ALL hypertensive patients, and continue even after drugs start.
Lifestyle alone lowers BP by about 5–10 mmHg; enough for some mild cases.
Salt under 6 g a day (one teaspoon); no added salt at the table.
Lose weight to a BMI under 25; each kilogram lost lowers systolic BP by about 1–2 mmHg.
Brisk walking 30 minutes a day.
Alcohol: at most 2 drinks a day for men, 1 for women. Stop smoking.
DASH diet: fruit, vegetables, low-fat dairy, less saturated fat.

sections.title: What you notice → what it means

lines.text: Hidden salt: bread, processed meat, cheese, packet soups, tomato paste.
Secondary causes (10–15%): kidney disease, thyroid disease, aldosterone excess, pregnancy.
Two cut-offs exist: ≥140/90 (WHO and Ethiopian national guideline) and ≥130/80 (2017 American guideline). Ethiopian exams generally use ≥140/90.
One high reading in clinic is not yet hypertension.
Treatment lowers stroke by 40–50% and heart attack by 16–30%.
Below 90/60 mmHg is hypotension.
A 45-year-old man has a BP of 150/95 mmHg at a routine visit. He has no symptoms and no previous readings. What is the most appropriate next step?
a. Start amlodipine today ✗: one reading is not enough to diagnose hypertension.
b. Repeat the BP on another day to confirm ✓: diagnosis needs raised readings on two different days.
c. Refer for emergency care ✗: he has no signs of an emergency.
d. Tell him the reading is normal ✗: 150/95 is raised and must be rechecked.

notes.title: Choosing a BP drug for the patient in front of you

lines.text: A hypertensive patient with one extra detail: pregnancy, diabetes, a cough on treatment, asthma, an enlarged prostate, gout, Black ethnicity, or an emergency. That detail decides the drug.
No other disease (Ethiopia) → start amlodipine; add a thiazide; third, an ACE inhibitor.
Pregnant → methyldopa, modified-release nifedipine, or a β-blocker in the third trimester.
Pregnant, or could become pregnant without contraception → NEVER ACE inhibitors, ARBs or thiazides.
Severe hypertension in pregnancy → IV labetalol or IV hydralazine. Seizures in pre-eclampsia → magnesium sulfate.
Diabetes or kidney disease → ACE inhibitor; it protects the kidneys.
Dry cough on an ACE inhibitor → switch to an ARB (losartan).
Young patient, fast heart rate, or angina → β-blocker.
Asthma or COPD → avoid non-selective β-blockers (propranolol).
Enlarged prostate (BPH) → α1-blocker (prazosin).
Gout → avoid thiazides.
Black patient → diuretic or CCB rather than ACE inhibitor or β-blocker.
Hypertensive emergency → IV sodium nitroprusside or labetalol.
ACE inhibitors and ARBs harm the fetus: low BP, no urine, kidney failure, malformation or death.
Amlodipine works in all races, needs little lab monitoring, and is safe for women who may become pregnant.
ACE inhibitors cause cough because bradykinin builds up; ARBs don't affect bradykinin.
ACE inhibitor + spironolactone or potassium supplements → dangerous hyperkalemia.
Angioedema (swollen lips, tongue, throat) on an ACE inhibitor → stop it and never restart.
Aliskiren together with an ACE inhibitor or ARB → contraindicated.
A 32-year-old woman at 24 weeks of pregnancy has BP 150/100 mmHg. She has taken lisinopril since before the pregnancy. What is the most appropriate change?
a. Continue lisinopril ✗: ACE inhibitors harm the fetus.
b. Switch to methyldopa ✓: the preferred BP drug in pregnancy.
c. Add hydrochlorothiazide ✗: thiazides are avoided in pregnancy.
d. Switch to losartan ✗: ARBs are also contraindicated in pregnancy.
A 56-year-old man with diabetes and hypertension has had a dry, tickly cough for a month since starting enalapril. What is the most appropriate action?
a. Add a cough syrup and continue enalapril ✗: treats the symptom, not the cause.
b. Switch to losartan ✓: ARBs give the same kidney protection without the bradykinin cough.
c. Stop all BP drugs ✗: his hypertension still needs treatment.
d. Switch to propranolol ✗: doesn't protect the kidneys; not the logical replacement.

notes.title: A BP patient with a new complaint: which drug caused it?

lines.text: A patient on BP treatment comes back with a new symptom. Match the symptom to the drug, then decide what to do.
Dry cough, loss of taste → ACE inhibitor (captopril, enalapril).
Swelling of lips, tongue or throat → ACE inhibitor angioedema: emergency; stop the drug.
Ankle swelling, headache, flushing → amlodipine or nifedipine.
Constipation → verapamil.
Dizziness or fainting on standing after the FIRST dose → prazosin (or the first ACE inhibitor dose).
Racing heart, sweating and very high BP after missing doses → clonidine rebound.
Sleepiness, low mood, dry mouth → methyldopa or clonidine.
Joint pain and rash like lupus → hydralazine.
Excess hair growth → minoxidil.
Slow pulse, cold hands, wheeze, hidden hypoglycemia → β-blocker.
Weakness and arrhythmia with high K⁺ → ACE inhibitor, ARB or spironolactone.
Give the first dose of prazosin at bedtime; tell the patient to rise slowly.
Never stop clonidine or a β-blocker suddenly; taper over days.
Check K⁺ and creatinine after starting an ACE inhibitor; a rise in creatinine up to 30% in the first days is expected.
Nitroprusside: protect the infusion from light (it forms cyanide).
Cough on an ACE inhibitor doesn't mean an infection; switch to an ARB.
A diabetic on propranolol may not feel hypoglycemia; the β-blocker hides the warning signs.
A 50-year-old woman started amlodipine 3 weeks ago. She now has swelling of both ankles but no breathlessness. What is the most likely cause?
a. Heart failure ✗: no breathlessness or crackles; the timing fits the drug.
b. Side effect of amlodipine ✓: dihydropyridine CCBs commonly cause ankle edema.
c. Kidney failure ✗: nothing else suggests kidney disease.
d. Allergy to amlodipine ✗: allergy would cause rash or angioedema, not ankle edema.
A man on clonidine forgot his tablets for two days. He now has a headache, sweating, palpitations and BP 200/120. What happened?
a. Clonidine overdose ✗: overdose lowers BP and causes sleepiness.
b. Rebound hypertension from stopping clonidine suddenly ✓: receptors are up-regulated; stopping causes a crisis.
c. Anxiety attack ✗: BP this high after missed clonidine is rebound until proven otherwise.
d. Normal variation ✗: 200/120 is a hypertensive crisis.

notes.title: Heart failure: what each drug is for

lines.text: A patient's heart can't pump enough: breathless, tired, swollen legs, crackles in the lungs, fast pulse. Some drugs relieve symptoms now; others help the patient live longer.
Fluid overload, swelling, breathlessness → diuretic (loop), the mainstay.
Long-term, to live longer → ACE inhibitor (ARB if not tolerated) + β-blocker (carvedilol, metoprolol, bisoprolol).
Weak heart with atrial fibrillation → digoxin (stronger, slower beat).
Acute severe heart failure in hospital → IV dobutamine (short term only).
Can't take an ACE inhibitor or β-blocker → hydralazine + isosorbide dinitrate.
Marked aldosterone excess → add spironolactone.

sections.title: What you notice → what it means

lines.text: Tachycardia, exercise intolerance, breathlessness, swelling, big heart → heart failure.
Main causes: ischemic heart disease, hypertension, valve disease, cardiomyopathy.
Daily weight; a gain of about 1–2 kg in a day or two means fluid is building up — report.
Before starting an ACE inhibitor, lower the diuretic dose to avoid low BP.
Position upright (high Fowler's) when breathless; limit salt and fluid as ordered.
The body's emergency responses (sympathetic system, RAAS, ADH) help at first but worsen the failing heart over time; ACE inhibitors and β-blockers block them.
β-blockers can worsen ACUTE heart failure but help CHRONIC heart failure.
Diuretics relieve symptoms but don't make the heart stronger.
Dobutamine is IV only, for a few days; tolerance after about 72 hours.
A 65-year-old woman with chronic heart failure asks which of her drugs will help her live longer. Which pair is correct?
a. Furosemide and digoxin ✗: they relieve symptoms but don't improve survival.
b. Enalapril and carvedilol ✓: ACE inhibitors and β-blockers improve survival in heart failure.
c. Dobutamine and furosemide ✗: dobutamine is short-term IV for acute failure.
d. Nifedipine and hydralazine ✗: not first-line heart failure drugs.

notes.title: Is this digoxin toxicity? What do you do?

lines.text: An older patient with heart failure or atrial fibrillation takes digoxin, usually with a diuretic such as furosemide. New symptoms, a slow pulse or a low potassium mean danger.

sections.title: What you notice → what it means

lines.text: Nausea, vomiting, visual disturbance → digoxin toxicity.
New irregular rhythm or slow pulse → toxicity reaching the heart.
Also on furosemide or a thiazide → expect LOW potassium.
Low K⁺ → a NORMAL dose becomes toxic. High Ca²⁺ does the same.
Low magnesium also raises toxicity.
Quinidine or verapamil added recently → digoxin level rises.
Amiodarone also raises digoxin levels.
Before every dose, count the apical pulse for one full minute; hold the dose if below 60 in an adult and report.
Signs of toxicity → hold digoxin (and the diuretic) and report.
Check K⁺, Ca²⁺ and the digoxin level; correct the electrolytes.
Slow heart rate → atropine. Arrhythmia → lidocaine. Severe toxicity → digoxin immune Fab (Digibind).
Digoxin blocks the Na⁺/K⁺ pump → more calcium inside heart cells → stronger beat; it also slows the heart through the vagus nerve.
Digoxin binds the pump's potassium site; less K⁺ leaves more sites free for digoxin.
“The dose was too low”: the dose didn't change, the potassium dropped.
“Give the scheduled dose” when the pulse is slow and vision has changed: never.
“Increase the furosemide”: it lowers potassium further.
Usual dose: 0.125–0.5 mg by mouth daily.
Hold if apical pulse < 60/min (adult).
Therapeutic serum level: about 0.5–2 ng/ml.
A 70-year-old man with heart failure takes digoxin and furosemide. He reports nausea and yellow halos. Pulse 54/min, irregular. K⁺ 2.8 mEq/L. What is the nurse's most appropriate action?
a. Give the morning digoxin dose as scheduled ✗: signs of toxicity, pulse below 60.
b. Hold digoxin and report; check potassium and digoxin level ✓: toxicity from low potassium; stop and correct.
c. Increase the furosemide ✗: lowers potassium further.
d. Reassure him that nausea is harmless ✗: nausea is an early toxicity sign.

notes.title: Chest pain: which angina, which drug, what first

lines.text: A patient has chest pain: pressing pain behind the sternum, often spreading to the left arm, shoulder or jaw. When and how it comes tells you the type, and the type decides the drug.
Pain on exertion, cold, eating or emotion, relieved by rest → stable angina → β-blocker, nitrate, CCB, aspirin, statin.
Pain at rest, often at night, from coronary spasm → variant (Prinzmetal) angina → CCB and nitrate; NOT a β-blocker.
Pain more often, with less effort or at rest → unstable angina → hospital: sublingual nitroglycerin, aspirin, anticoagulant, oxygen if saturation is low.
Any acute attack → sublingual nitroglycerin.
Stop activity; sit the patient down; give sublingual nitroglycerin as ordered.
Nitroglycerin can be repeated every 5 minutes, up to 3 doses; if pain isn't better after the first dose, call for emergency help.
Low-dose aspirin daily for stable and unstable angina, unless allergic or bleeding.
Check BP before nitrates; they can cause sudden hypotension.
Angina = the heart muscle needs more oxygen than it gets. Drugs either lower demand (β-blockers, CCBs, nitrates) or improve supply (nitrates, CCBs).
Unstable angina comes from small clots on a cracked plaque, so antiplatelets and anticoagulants are key.
Variant angina + propranolol: wrong; β-blockers don't help spasm.
Never stop a β-blocker suddenly; it can trigger a heart attack.
Unstable angina is an emergency (acute coronary syndrome), not a clinic follow-up.
Aspirin for angina: 80–325 mg daily.
Clopidogrel: 300 mg loading dose, then 75 mg daily.
Sublingual nitroglycerin works in 2–3 minutes and lasts about 2 hours.
A 48-year-old woman has chest pain that wakes her at night, at rest. ECG during pain shows changes that return to normal. Exercise testing is normal. Which drug is most appropriate for prevention?
a. Propranolol ✗: β-blockers are not useful in variant angina.
b. A calcium channel blocker ✓: most effective prevention of coronary spasm (variant angina).
c. Furosemide ✗: not an antianginal.
d. Digoxin ✗: not an antianginal.
A 62-year-old man with known stable angina says his chest pain now comes several times a day, even when sitting. What is the most appropriate action?
a. Increase his walking to build tolerance ✗: worsening pain at rest means danger.
b. Refer urgently: this is unstable angina ✓: unstable angina needs hospital admission and aggressive treatment.
c. Reassure and review in a month ✗: risk of heart attack and death.
d. Stop his aspirin ✗: aspirin is essential in unstable angina.

notes.title: Giving nitrates safely

lines.text: A patient uses nitroglycerin for angina, under the tongue for attacks or as tablets or patches for prevention. The nurse teaches correct use and watches for hypotension.
Acute attack → sublingual nitroglycerin (not swallowed).
Prevention → long-acting tablets or patches, with a daily nitrate-free period.
Taking sildenafil (Viagra) → nitrates contraindicated: dangerous hypotension.
Teach: sit down before taking it; it can make you dizzy.
A throbbing headache is expected; it usually eases with time.
Keep tablets in their original dark glass bottle, away from heat and light.
Remove the patch for some hours each day (often overnight) to prevent tolerance.
Nitrates become nitric oxide, which mainly widens veins → less blood returns to the heart → less work and less oxygen needed.
Swallowed nitrates are mostly destroyed by the liver (first-pass effect); under the tongue they skip it.
Headache after nitroglycerin is NOT a reason to stop it.
Continuous patches without a break → tolerance, the drug stops working.
Stopping long-term nitrates suddenly can cause severe ischemia.
A man using nitroglycerin patches for angina asks whether he can take sildenafil for erectile problems. What is the nurse's best response?
a. Yes, at a lower dose ✗: even a low dose can cause severe hypotension.
b. No, together they can cause a dangerous fall in BP ✓: sildenafil with nitrates is contraindicated.
c. Yes, if he removes the patch an hour before ✗: still dangerous; needs the prescriber's decision.
d. Only if his BP is high ✗: the combination is contraindicated regardless.

notes.title: Arrhythmia drugs: which one for which rhythm

lines.text: A patient has a fast, slow or irregular heartbeat. The rhythm decides the drug, and some antiarrhythmics have side effects the nurse must watch for.
Sudden fast narrow rhythm (paroxysmal SVT) → adenosine IV, drug of choice.
Atrial fibrillation → slow the rate with verapamil/diltiazem, a β-blocker or digoxin.
Ventricular arrhythmia after MI or heart surgery → lidocaine IV.
Any arrhythmia when others fail → amiodarone.
Torsades de pointes → magnesium sulfate.
Slow heart rate (e.g. digoxin toxicity) → atropine.

sections.title: What you notice → what it means

lines.text: Cough and breathlessness on amiodarone → lung fibrosis.
Blue-gray skin, sunburn easily, eye deposits, thyroid problems on amiodarone → amiodarone toxicity.
Ringing ears, blurred vision, GI upset on quinidine → cinchonism.
Confusion or seizures on lidocaine → CNS toxicity.
Lupus-like rash and joint pain on procainamide → slow acetylator reaction.
Adenosine: rapid IV push followed by a saline flush; warn the patient about brief flushing and breathlessness.
Before and during amiodarone, check thyroid, liver and lung function.
Monitor ECG and pulse when giving antiarrhythmics.
Class I block sodium, II are β-blockers, III block potassium (amiodarone), IV block calcium (verapamil).
Adenosine lasts under 10 seconds, so it must be given fast.
Verapamil + β-blocker or digoxin → risk of AV block.
Lidocaine isn't given by mouth: destroyed by the liver (first pass).
Low potassium itself can cause arrhythmias.
Theophylline blocks adenosine's effect.
Normal heart rate 60–100. Flutter 250–350; fibrillation over 350.
Amiodarone half-life: over 80 days.
A 30-year-old woman has sudden palpitations. Pulse 190/min, regular, narrow-complex tachycardia; BP is stable. Vagal maneuvers failed. Which drug is the nurse most likely to prepare?
a. Adenosine IV ✓: drug of choice for paroxysmal SVT.
b. Atropine IV ✗: speeds the heart; used for bradycardia.
c. Magnesium sulfate ✗: for torsades de pointes.
d. Digoxin by mouth ✗: too slow for an acute attack.
A man on long-term amiodarone develops a dry cough and increasing breathlessness. What should the nurse suspect?
a. Asthma ✗: new cough on amiodarone points to the drug.
b. Pulmonary fibrosis from amiodarone ✓: a known serious toxicity.
c. ACE inhibitor cough ✗: he is on amiodarone, not an ACE inhibitor.
d. Normal aging ✗: new breathlessness needs investigation.

notes.title: Statins and other lipid drugs: safe use

lines.text: A patient with high LDL cholesterol, angina or a past heart attack takes a statin. The nurse watches for muscle and liver damage.
High LDL, after MI, unstable angina → statin (atorvastatin, simvastatin, rosuvastatin), first line.
Mainly high triglycerides → fibrate (gemfibrozil, fenofibrate) or omega-3.
Can't tolerate a statin → ezetimibe, bile acid binders, niacin.
Pregnant or breastfeeding → no statins.

sections.title: What you notice → what it means

lines.text: Muscle pain, weakness, dark urine on a statin → myopathy or rhabdomyolysis; check CK.
Jaundice, raised liver enzymes → statin liver toxicity.
Flushing and itching on niacin → expected; aspirin beforehand helps.
Gallstones on a fibrate.
Report muscle pain or dark urine at once.
Check liver tests and CK as ordered.
Give bile acid binders apart from other oral drugs (they block warfarin, digoxin, thiazides).
Statins block HMG-CoA reductase, so the liver makes less cholesterol and pulls more LDL out of the blood.
Statin + gemfibrozil → higher risk of rhabdomyolysis.
Bile acid binders raise triglycerides; avoid when triglycerides are high.
Statins lower LDL by up to 60%.
After MI, aggressive cholesterol lowering cuts cardiovascular death by about 42%.
A 58-year-old man started atorvastatin and gemfibrozil 2 weeks ago. He now has severe muscle pain and dark brown urine. What is the priority?
a. Give paracetamol for the pain ✗: misses a dangerous drug reaction.
b. Hold the drugs, report, and check CK and kidney function ✓: suspected rhabdomyolysis; worse with gemfibrozil.
c. Encourage more exercise ✗: worsens muscle damage.
d. Increase the statin dose ✗: harmful.

notes.title: Ulcer & heartburn: choosing the drug

lines.text: A patient has epigastric pain, heartburn or a confirmed ulcer. The cause (H. pylori, NSAIDs) and how strong acid control must be decide the drug.
Quick relief of heartburn → antacid (aluminium + magnesium).
Strongest acid control (ulcer, GERD, Zollinger-Ellison) → PPI (omeprazole).
Night-time acid → H2 blocker (ranitidine, famotidine) works especially well.
Ulcer from NSAIDs, prevention or treatment → PPI (or misoprostol, but never in pregnancy).
H. pylori ulcer → triple therapy: PPI + amoxicillin + clarithromycin for 14 days (metronidazole if penicillin-allergic).
Triple therapy fails or not suitable → quadruple: bismuth + metronidazole + tetracycline + PPI.
Coat and protect the ulcer → sucralfate or bismuth.
Advise: stop smoking; avoid alcohol, caffeine, cola drinks.
Stress the full H. pylori course; stopping early leads to failure and resistance.
Ask every woman of childbearing age about pregnancy before misoprostol.
Acid is switched on by acetylcholine, gastrin and histamine, and made by the proton pump. PPIs block the pump itself (90–98% of acid); H2 blockers block one signal (60–70%).
Misoprostol in pregnancy → can cause abortion or birth defects.
Black tongue and stools on bismuth → harmless; not bleeding.
Long-standing GERD → Barrett's esophagus, a cancer risk.
A 40-year-old has a duodenal ulcer and a positive H. pylori test. He is allergic to penicillin. Which regimen is most appropriate?
a. PPI + amoxicillin + clarithromycin ✗: amoxicillin is a penicillin.
b. PPI + metronidazole + clarithromycin ✓: metronidazole replaces amoxicillin in penicillin allergy.
c. Antacid alone ✗: doesn't eradicate H. pylori.
d. Misoprostol alone ✗: doesn't eradicate H. pylori.
A pregnant woman with an NSAID-related stomach ulcer needs treatment. Which drug must be avoided?
a. Omeprazole ✗: not the main concern here.
b. Misoprostol ✓: contraindicated in pregnancy; can cause abortion.
c. Antacid ✗: commonly used.
d. Sucralfate ✗: acts locally.

notes.title: Diarrhea & constipation: choosing the drug

lines.text: A patient has diarrhea or constipation. Choose a drug by what's happening in the bowel, and know which effects are harmless.
Diarrhea needing the bowel slowed → loperamide (or diphenoxylate).
Traveler's diarrhea → bismuth subsalicylate.
Hard stools, straining → stool softener (docusate) or lubricant (glycerin suppository).
Long-term constipation, low fiber → bulk laxative (psyllium, bran) with plenty of water.
Quick bowel clearing → stimulant (senna, bisacodyl) or osmotic (magnesium hydroxide).
Dehydration from diarrhea → oral rehydration first; drugs come second.
Teach: bismuth makes stools and tongue black; harmless.
Adsorbents (aluminium hydroxide, methylcellulose) bind other drugs; space doses apart.
Laxatives can reduce the effect of slow-release tablets by rushing them through.
A patient taking bismuth subsalicylate for traveler's diarrhea is worried because his stools are black. What should the nurse say?
a. This is internal bleeding; go to the emergency room ✗: bismuth causes harmless black stools.
b. Black stools are an expected, harmless effect of bismuth ✓: correct.
c. Stop the drug and start loperamide ✗: not needed.
d. Black stools mean the diarrhea is getting worse ✗: unrelated.

notes.title: Treating TB & leprosy: regimen and adherence

lines.text: A patient is diagnosed with TB (or leprosy) and starts months of treatment. Success depends on several drugs together and taking every dose.
Always several drugs together → a single drug lets resistance develop quickly.
First-line: isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide, ethambutol (streptomycin when an injection is needed).
Pyrazinamide with INH and rifampin makes a 6-month course possible.
Latent TB (positive skin test) or HIV patients → isoniazid preventive therapy.
Resistant (MDR) TB → second-line: fluoroquinolones (moxifloxacin), amikacin, capreomycin, cycloserine, ethionamide.
Leprosy → dapsone + clofazimine + rifampin for 6–24 months.
Directly observe dose-taking where possible; stress never skipping doses.
Give pyridoxine with isoniazid to prevent neuropathy, especially in diabetes, HIV, malnutrition, alcoholism.
Check liver tests; teach the signs of hepatitis (jaundice, dark urine).
TB grows slowly, hides inside cells and has a tough wall, so treatment must be long and combined.
Cycloserine in a patient with epilepsy or depression → seizures, psychosis, suicide risk.
Dapsone → hemolysis and methemoglobinemia.
A man with TB feels better after 3 weeks and wants to stop his tablets. What is the nurse's best response?
a. Stop, since symptoms are gone ✗: early stopping causes relapse and resistance.
b. Continue the full course; stopping early causes relapse and drug resistance ✓: correct.
c. Take only isoniazid from now ✗: single-drug treatment causes resistance.
d. Take the tablets only when coughing ✗: irregular use causes resistance.

notes.title: A TB patient with a new complaint: which drug, what to do

lines.text: A patient on TB treatment comes with a new symptom. Match the symptom to the drug, then act.
Burning or numb feet and hands → isoniazid neuropathy → pyridoxine (vitamin B6).
Orange urine, sweat or tears → rifampin; harmless, reassure.
Blurred vision or trouble telling red from green → ethambutol; report.
Joint pain, high uric acid, gout → pyrazinamide.
Jaundice, dark urine, loss of appetite → hepatitis (isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide); report.
Hearing loss or ringing in the ears on an injectable (streptomycin, amikacin, capreomycin) → ototoxicity; report.
Woman on the pill starts rifampin → contraceptive failure; she needs another method.
Isoniazid causes a relative B6 deficiency, more in slow acetylators, malnutrition, alcoholism, diabetes, AIDS.
Rifampin strongly speeds the liver, so pills, anticoagulants and HIV drugs are cleared faster.
Stopping all TB drugs for orange urine: wrong; it's harmless.
Ethambutol in a child too young to report vision problems: avoided.
A 35-year-old diabetic on TB treatment for 6 weeks has burning and numbness in both feet. What is the most appropriate intervention?
a. Give pyridoxine (vitamin B6) as ordered ✓: isoniazid neuropathy; diabetes raises the risk.
b. Stop all TB drugs ✗: managed with B6, not by stopping treatment.
c. Tell him it's from rifampin ✗: rifampin causes orange fluids.
d. Check his color vision ✗: that's for ethambutol.
A woman on combined oral contraceptives starts TB treatment. What should the nurse teach?
a. No change is needed ✗: rifampin can make the pill fail.
