b. Use an additional or different contraceptive method ✓: rifampin speeds the breakdown of the pill's hormones.
c. Stop TB treatment while on the pill ✗: TB treatment must continue.
d. Double the pill dose ✗: not the recommended approach.

notes.title: Choosing contraception for a woman

lines.text: A woman asks for family planning. One detail about her (breastfeeding, days since delivery, smoking, an illness, another drug) decides which method is safe.
Breastfeeding → progestin-only (mini pill, injection, implant). No combined (estrogen) methods.
Postpartum, NOT breastfeeding, under 21 days → still no estrogen (clot risk is high); progestin-only is safe.
Over 35 AND smoking → no combined method; choose progestin-only.
Migraine, hypertension, past clot, liver disease, heart failure → no combined method.
Fibroids → mini pill rather than the combined pill.
On rifampin, phenytoin or phenobarbital → the pill may fail; add or switch method.
Wants 3 months of protection without daily pills → depot medroxyprogesterone 150 mg IM every 3 months.
Wants protection for years → implant (3–5 years) or IUD.
Copper IUD within 5 days → the most effective emergency method.
Levonorgestrel-based pills → within 72 hours (best within 12).
Mifepristone ± misoprostol → up to 120 hours.
Estrogen raises the risk of thromboembolism and hypertension.
Progestin-only methods avoid estrogen's risks but fail slightly more often.
Combined pill or ring for a woman 2 weeks after delivery: estrogen → wrong before 21 days.
Female sterilization for a young woman who only wants spacing: permanent → not “most appropriate”.
Thromboembolism on the pill → estrogen. Ectopic pregnancy, weight gain, low mood → progestin.
A 28-year-old multiparous woman is 14 days postpartum and not breastfeeding. She has no chronic disease. What is the most appropriate contraceptive method?
a. Progestin-only injectable ✓: safe right after delivery; no estrogen.
b. Combined oral contraceptive ✗: estrogen before 21 days postpartum.
c. Female sterilization ✗: permanent; nothing suggests she wants that.
d. Combined vaginal ring ✗: also contains estrogen.
A 30-year-old woman had unprotected sex 4 days ago. Which is the most effective emergency contraception?
a. Levonorgestrel pills ✗: best within 72 hours; less effective at 4 days.
b. Copper IUD insertion ✓: most effective, works up to 5 days.
c. Combined pill started today ✗: not emergency contraception.
d. Condoms from now on ✗: doesn't prevent pregnancy from the past act.

notes.title: The woman on the pill: instructions & problems

lines.text: A woman is using the combined pill, mini pill or another hormonal method. The nurse teaches correct use and recognizes side effects and danger signs.
Monthly combined pill: 21 days (day 5 to 26), then 7 pill-free days; 28-pill packs include 7 sugar pills.
Seasonal pill: 84 days on, 7 off; 4 periods a year; more spotting early.
Mini pill: every day at the same time, all year, no break.
Patch: weekly for 3 weeks, 1 week off. Ring: 3 weeks in, 1 out.

sections.title: What you notice → what it means

lines.text: Nausea, breast tenderness, headache, skin darkening → estrogen effects.
Weight gain, low mood, irregular bleeding, acne, hirsutism → progestin effects.
Calf pain and swelling, chest pain, breathlessness, severe headache → possible clot: stop and seek care urgently.
Raised BP on the pill → estrogen effect.
Check BP before and during combined pill use.
Ask about all other drugs; enzyme inducers cause pill failure.
The pill raises warfarin, cyclosporine and theophylline levels.
Missing the timing of the mini pill matters more than with the combined pill (slightly higher failure).
A woman on the combined pill for 6 months has pain and swelling of one calf. What is the most likely concern?
a. Muscle strain ✗: the pill raises clot risk.
b. Deep vein thrombosis from estrogen ✓: estrogen increases thromboembolism.
c. Progestin side effect ✗: progestin effects are weight gain, mood change.
d. Normal pill effect ✗: this is a danger sign.

notes.title: Skin problems: choosing & teaching the drug

lines.text: A patient has acne, psoriasis, vitiligo or a skin infection. Most treatment is applied to the skin, but some drugs have serious body-wide risks.
Mild to moderate acne without inflammation → benzoyl peroxide.
Comedones and inflammatory acne → topical retinoid (adapalene).
Inflamed acne → topical clindamycin (with benzoyl peroxide or a retinoid); oral doxycycline if moderate–severe.
Severe cystic acne only → oral isotretinoin.
Mild psoriasis → topical steroid, vitamin D analogue (calcipotriene), tazarotene; scalp → coal tar or salicylic acid.
Vitiligo → methoxsalen + UVA (PUVA). Dark patches (melasma) → hydroquinone.
Impetigo, including MRSA → mupirocin.
Minor cuts and burns → bacitracin or the triple antibiotic ointment.
Before any retinoid: pregnancy test and reliable contraception.
Isotretinoin: watch mood; report depression or suicidal thoughts.
Use less on the face, scalp, armpits and groin; they absorb much more.
Covering the skin with plastic (occlusion) greatly increases the effect; only when ordered.
Retinoids in pregnancy → contraindicated.
Alcohol with acitretin → converts it to a longer-lasting toxic form.
Bacitracin is toxic if given systemically.
A 22-year-old woman with severe cystic acne is to start oral isotretinoin. What is the most important nursing action first?
a. Teach her to wash her face more often ✗: doesn't address the main risk.
b. Confirm she is not pregnant and uses reliable contraception ✓: isotretinoin causes birth defects.
c. Apply benzoyl peroxide together ✗: not the priority.
d. Advise sun exposure ✗: retinoids cause photosensitivity.
